clue.text: Often what businessman wants?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: frequently, lots of the time
second meaning: a very good bargain, which any trader hopes to strike

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading: the phrase means 'frequently' as an adverb, and read literally it is a superb bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom works as an adverb of frequency, and taken word by word it names an excellent commercial agreement.

clue.text: Oddly, a surreal atmosphere

indicators.note: odd here means the odd-numbered positions, so take the first, third, fifth and so on

parts.note: letters one, three, five and seven of the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone senses something strangely dreamlike in the air of a place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' reads as an adverb for the strangeness, but it asks for the odd-placed letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An aura is the distinctive feeling or mood surrounding a person or place, a close synonym.

clue.text: Remember convoluted Celtic lore? Not I

indicators.note: something convoluted is twisted and tangled, so the letters are jumbled
'not' tells you to leave out the letter that follows it from the material

parts.note: taken as written, ten letters
the letter to be dropped from the ten

explanation.surface: Someone is asked whether they recall tangled Celtic myths, and answers that they do not.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the I from the two words first, leaving nine letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To recollect is to call something back to mind, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: Sound from car phone, essentially

parts.note: Audi is a German car make

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so take the letter at the very centre of the word

parts.note: the central letter of a five-letter word

explanation.surface: A noise is coming through the speakers of a hands-free car phone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Car' is a cue for a make of car rather than a vehicle in general.
explanation.definitionFit: Audio means relating to recorded or transmitted sound, so it is a fair stand-in for the noun used attributively.

clue.text: Lower frock, holding base softly

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so one part sits inside the other

parts.note: a frock is a dress
e is the base of natural logarithms in mathematics
p, piano, is the musical marking for soft

explanation.surface: Someone lets down the hem of a frock, keeping the soft base fabric in place.
explanation.walkthrough: Base as e comes from maths: the natural logarithm uses base e.
explanation.definitionFit: To depress is to press down or push lower, so both are transitive verbs of moving downward.

clue.text: Strait's affected those working with oils?

indicators.note: something affected has been altered or changed, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: the possessive read as plain letters, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A narrow sea channel has been fouled, harming the crews who work around oil spills.
explanation.walkthrough: Oils suggests an oil slick at sea; the question mark signals oil paints instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Painters work in oil paints, so 'those working with oils' describes painters by example.

clue.text: Wild American president

definitions.meaning: first meaning: uncultivated wilderness, as in the Australian outback
second meaning: either of the two US presidents of that surname

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like an adjective describing a president, but 'Wild' is a noun for untamed country.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names untamed scrubland country and is also the surname of two US presidents, father and son.

clue.text: Carol, with uniform on, is working

indicators.note: 'with' simply sets one element alongside another; 'on' in a down clue puts it on top

parts.note: U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to carol is to sing

explanation.surface: A woman called Carol has put on her work uniform and is on shift.
explanation.walkthrough: Carol is a name in the surface but a verb in the wordplay; in a down clue 'on' places the U above.
explanation.definitionFit: Working a machine or using it both mean operating or employing it, so the participles match.

clue.text: Hold son, possibly?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a wrestling grip on an opponent's arm and neck

definitions.note: describes the word 'son' rather than meaning it
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the three letters s-o-n are the back half of the admiral's surname Nelson

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading: 'son' is literally one half of the word Nelson.
explanation.definitionFit: This wrestling grip pins an opponent by an arm hooked under theirs and a hand pressed on the neck.

clue.text: Deduce French couturier lacking diamonds is lower in status

parts.note: to deduce is to infer

indicators.note: lacking something means going without it, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: Christian Dior, the Paris fashion designer
D is the abbreviation for diamonds in card games

explanation.surface: One concludes that a Paris fashion house without its jewels has lost prestige.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the D from DIOR before adding it to the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Inferior describes someone of lesser rank or standing, an adjective synonym for the phrase.

clue.text: Put one's foot down crack in road

indicators.note: 'in' places one part inside the other, here the word for crack sits within the road abbreviation

parts.note: RD is the standard abbreviation for road, as in street addresses
crack as an adjective means first-rate or expert, as in a crack shot, and so does ace

explanation.surface: A driver stamps on the pedal over a crack in the road surface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' reads as a split in the tarmac, but it is the adjective for top-class, as in crack troops; 'in' then puts it inside the road.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting your foot down on the accelerator means driving very fast, so the past-tense idiom matches sped or raced.

clue.text: Powerful current? A lifeboat initially is likely

parts.note: potent means powerful
I is the symbol for electric current in physics
taken as written

indicators.note: initially points to the start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A strong sea current is running, so a lifeboat launch looks probable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' suggests the sea; in the wordplay it is the physics symbol I.
explanation.definitionFit: A potential problem is one that could plausibly arise, so the adjective means possible or probable.

clue.text: Boobs — you might see these in bed

definitions.meaning: first meaning: boobs are silly mistakes, gaffes

definitions.text: you might see these in bed
definitions.meaning: second meaning: flowering plants growing in a flower bed, with a nod to old-fashioned knickers

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is cheeky, but a boob is a blunder and the bed is a garden flower bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloomer is informal British for an embarrassing error, and plants in flower are things that bloom.

clue.text: Prod food with leg

indicators.note: 'with' sets one element alongside the next, joining them

parts.note: an egg is an item of food
in cricket the leg side of the field is also called the on side

explanation.surface: Someone pokes at their meal with a chicken leg.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket, the British bat-and-ball game, names the half of the field behind a batter's legs both 'leg' and 'on'.
explanation.definitionFit: To prod someone is to urge or encourage them, which is what the phrasal verb means.

clue.text: Noted Beetle car broken down to begin with

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so the letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written, nine letters

indicators.note: this phrase points to the start, so only the opening letter is used

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A famous Volkswagen Beetle has broken down at the start of a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beetle car' looks like the famous Volkswagen model, but both words are anagram material.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted and celebrated both describe someone famous and widely admired, adjective synonyms.

clue.text: Foes somewhat close? I'm energetically retreating!

indicators.note: something retreating goes backwards, so the letters run the other way
somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the text is used

parts.note: letters spanning the end of the first word, the middle word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone sees their rivals getting nearer and runs away fast.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the string backwards from the punctuation onwards; the question mark and apostrophe are ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Foes and enemies are both opponents or adversaries, a plain plural synonym.

clue.text: Lettuces? These are to be avoided in the main

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a crisp, round variety of salad leaf

definitions.text: These are to be avoided in the main
definitions.meaning: second meaning: floating masses of frozen water that ships must steer clear of; 'the main' is the open sea

explanation.walkthrough: 'In the main' sounds like 'mostly', but it is a poetic name for the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: The variety of lettuce shares its name with the huge drifting blocks of ice that endanger ships at sea.

clue.text: One large female wearing crown, nearly polished

indicators.note: something worn sits on top of or around the wearer, so one part goes inside another
nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: the crown is the top of the head, so the skull
the Roman numeral for one
L is the standard abbreviation for large
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A big woman in a crown looks almost glossy and refined.
explanation.walkthrough: Trim the head-bone word to SKUL first, then put the three letters inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A polished performance is accomplished and expert, so the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Still on X? Editor's deflated

indicators.note: 'on' in a down clue places one element directly above the next

parts.note: a still drink, with no fizz, is flat
X is the Roman numeral for ten
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor; the apostrophe-s that follows is a link meaning 'is'

explanation.surface: An editor feels deflated at still being stuck on Twitter, now called X.
explanation.walkthrough: X looks like the social network, but it is the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Deflated and flattened both describe being crushed or knocked down in spirits, past-participle synonyms.

clue.text: Most violent trembles removing bottom half in river

indicators.note: removing the bottom half means dropping the second part of the word
something in another thing is enclosed by it

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, south-west England
the first four of its eight letters

explanation.surface: Someone shudders hardest of all as they lose their lower half in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue the 'bottom' half is the end of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Extreme means at the furthest, most intense degree, so it matches the superlative of violent.

clue.text: Describe old scheme involving India

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: to involve is to include within, so one part takes in another

parts.note: a scheme is a plan
I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to outline a historic colonial project in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' gives the prefix EX, which goes in front of the scheme with India inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To describe something is to give an account of it, which is close to explaining it.

clue.text: Rank odorant wind

indicators.note: to rank things is to put them in a new order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A foul-smelling substance accompanies some flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' as an adjective means smelly, which suits odorant; it is really the verb for ordering.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a violent rotating windstorm, so it is an example of wind.

clue.text: One delivering lessons in school term, almost without anguish

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut
without in its old sense means outside, so one part wraps around another

parts.note: the word less its final letter
an ache is anguish or pain

explanation.surface: A schoolteacher gets through nearly the whole term free of distress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'free of', but here it means outside; 'in school' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacher is a person who gives lessons to pupils, so the descriptive phrase defines the job.

clue.text: Search everywhere around lake

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one part encloses another

parts.note: rife means widespread, found everywhere
L is the abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: Someone hunts all over the area surrounding a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Everywhere' must be turned into an adjective meaning widespread before it can hold the L.
explanation.definitionFit: To rifle through something is to search it hurriedly, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Wrong answer admitted by fine university

indicators.note: something admitted is let in, so it goes inside the other part

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads
A is the abbreviation for answer
the LSE is the London School of Economics

explanation.surface: A respected university accepts a candidate who gave an incorrect answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine university' looks like praise for one institution; it is F followed by the LSE, the London School of Economics.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrong and false both mean incorrect or untrue, plain adjective synonyms.

clue.text: Nice large shed primarily suits agricultural labourers

indicators.note: to shed something is to cast it off, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: nice means pleasant
L is the abbreviation for large

indicators.note: primarily points to what comes first, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A large shed in Nice, the French city, is mostly fitted out for farm workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' at the start looks like the French city, but it is the adjective; 'shed' is a verb, not a hut.
explanation.definitionFit: Peasants are poor farm workers who work the land, the traditional sense of the plural noun.

clue.text: Saw bad cage with no openings

indicators.note: an opening is a beginning, so each word loses its first letter

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sees a nasty cage with no doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see, but it is a noun for an old saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw in this old sense is a proverb or maxim, which is exactly what an adage is.

clue.text: Runs Cambridgeshire city bank

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, England

explanation.surface: Someone operates a bank in a Cambridgeshire city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' is the verb, as in banking on something, not a financial institution.
explanation.definitionFit: To bank on someone is to depend on them, so as a verb it means count or depend.

clue.text: The large criminal carrying piano wire

indicators.note: to carry is to hold within, so one letter is taken inside
criminal means crooked, so the letters are bent out of their order

parts.note: taken as written
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, soft

explanation.surface: A big crook is carrying piano wire, the classic weapon of a strangler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piano wire' looks like one item, but piano is just P and wire is the definition, also the name of this newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: To wire someone in the old sense is to send a telegram, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Italian niece partly musical

indicators.note: partly means only in part, so a section of the text is used

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the second

explanation.surface: A girl's Italian niece has some musical talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical' looks like an adjective describing the niece, but it is the noun for a stage show.
explanation.definitionFit: The stage show about an orphan girl, with the song Tomorrow, is a well-known Broadway musical.

clue.text: Carries out birds, very withdrawn

indicators.note: something withdrawn has been taken away, so a letter is removed

parts.note: doves are birds
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: Someone takes birds outside, who are very shy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Withdrawn' reads like shy birds; it tells you to take the V out.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry out a task is to perform it, so the third-person verbs match.

clue.text: Frosty funnel I dry at sea

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are muddled

parts.note: taken as written, ten letters

explanation.surface: A ship's funnel stays icy but dry out on the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' fits the ship's funnel picture, but it signals a jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A frosty reception is cold and hostile, so the word figuratively means lacking warmth.
